title: H-1B Workers Face 60-Day Countdown as Tech Layoffs Intensify in 2026
excerpt: With over 110,000 tech jobs cut this year and a proposed rule to eliminate the grace period entirely, Indian visa holders are scrambling for alternatives.
body:
• More than 110,000 tech employees across 144 companies have been laid off in 2026, with Indian nationals accounting for the majority of H-1B holders affected.
  • Laid-off H-1B workers have a 60-day grace period from their last working day to find a new sponsor, switch visa categories, or leave the country.
  • The Department of Homeland Security is advancing a proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period entirely, which would mean immediate consequences for workers' legal status after a layoff.
  • Immigration attorneys report a significant increase in denials and requests for additional evidence on change-of-status applications filed by laid-off workers.

The wave of tech layoffs sweeping through Silicon Valley in 2026 is hitting Indian H-1B visa holders with particular force, as thousands face a 60-day window to secure new employment or uproot lives built over years — sometimes decades — in the United States.

According to Layoffs.fyi, more than 110,000 employees across 144 technology companies have lost their jobs this year. Meta alone has cut around 8,000 positions globally as it redirects resources toward artificial intelligence. Amazon, LinkedIn, Oracle, and Cisco have also trimmed headcount significantly.

The 60-Day Clock

Under current US Citizenship and Immigration Services rules, laid-off H-1B workers have 60 days from their last working day — not their final paycheck — to find a new employer willing to sponsor their visa, switch to another visa category, or prepare to leave the country.

https://x.com/Polymarket/status/2088129991561052285

The distinction between last working day and last pay date is critical and often misunderstood. Severance packages, COBRA continuation, and internal transitions do not extend H-1B status, meaning the clock may start ticking before workers realize it.

"Families are now dealing with mortgage payments, apartment leases, children in schools, and uncertain immigration timelines all at once, with only 60 days to resolve it."

— Rajiv Khanna, US-based immigration attorney

Grace Period Under Threat

The situation could worsen. The Department of Homeland Security is advancing a proposed rule (RIN: 1615-AD22) to eliminate the 60-day grace period entirely. The proposal, which has been sent to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review, would mean immediate consequences for workers' legal status if they are affected by layoffs.

The grace period was introduced in 2017 specifically to give H-1B workers time to transition after losing employment. Removing it would eliminate the last buffer between a layoff notice and potential deportation proceedings.

Shrinking Options

Traditionally, laid-off H-1B workers could apply for B-1 or B-2 visitor visas as a stopgap while job hunting. But immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna told the Economic Times that his team is seeing a significant spike in requests for additional evidence and notices of intent to deny on change-of-status applications — at a scale he described as unprecedented in his career.

Some workers are exploring F-1 student visas, O-1 extraordinary ability visas, and L-1 intra-company transfer routes. Canada's Express Entry and Global Talent Stream programmes are also attracting growing interest from Indian professionals evaluating their options.

Deep Roots at Risk

Indians represent the single largest group of H-1B holders, accounting for 283,772 of the 406,348 approved H-1B petitions in fiscal year 2025, according to USCIS and DHS data. Many have spent years or even decades in the US waiting for green cards due to per-country caps on permanent employment-based visas.

A Blind poll cited in media reports suggested nearly half of Indian professionals in the US would consider returning to India if they lost their jobs. For those with US-born children, home loans, and established careers, the calculus goes far beyond employment.

Meta has offered affected employees severance covering 16 weeks of base pay plus two additional weeks per year of service, alongside 18 months of healthcare coverage. But for H-1B holders, the core problem remains: severance does not extend visa status.
